originalTitle: Asia stocks slide as AI rout deepens despite rebound in U.S. futures
summary: Investing.com -- Asian stocks fell on Monday as renewed selling in technology and semiconductor shares deepened concerns over AI valuations and the mounting debt used to finance data-centre investments, even as U.S. equity futures rebounded following Wall Street's sharp weekly losses.
content:
Investing.com -- Asian stocks fell on Monday as renewed selling in technology and semiconductor shares deepened concerns over AI valuations and the mounting debt used to finance data-centre investments, even as U.S. equity futures rebounded following Wall Street's sharp weekly losses.

South Korea's KOSPI plunged 5%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.5% and Taiwan's Weighted Index rose 0.5%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained 2.5% and S&P 500 futures advanced 2% in Asian trade.

On Friday, the S&P 500 entered correction after a seventh straight loss; the Dow fell 1.9%, more than 10% below its peak. The Nasdaq sank 5.3% turning negative for 2026. The Dow and S&P 500 fell 8% and 8.6% for the week, their steepest weekly losses since April 2025, while the Nasdaq's 10% weekly slide was its biggest since March 2020.

Nvidia tumbled 14%, Anthropic 8.5% on its second day of trading and the Philadelphia semiconductor index about 11%. The VIX reached its highest level since April 2025.

The AI rally had also lifted switch, cable and power suppliers. Investors now doubt debt-funded data-centre builds will earn enough to repay lenders or justify valuations; Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, Anthropic's weak post-IPO trading and higher rates have deepened the rout.

Asian markets slide as policymakers prepare support measures

The MSCI Asia-Pacific gauge excluding Japan fell 0.7%, nearing bear-market territory after losing about 18% from its June peak.

Emerging-market stocks risked giving up their 2026 gains. Taiwan shares rose 0.5% after a 17% weekly plunge, the steepest since 1990. The KOSPI fell to a 10-month low of 4,632.34, while the Hang Seng lost 330.80 points. China's CSI 300 and Shanghai Composite lost 1.1% and 1.5%.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.1%, New Zealand's NZX 50 fell 1.7% and Singapore's Straits Times Index declined 1.4%. Gift Nifty futures gained 0.3%. Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

Authorities moved to contain the selloff. Taiwan tightened short-selling rules and has also been buying shares. South Korea is preparing to activate a stabilisation fund, last used in 2008, immediately if needed; it will ease listed companies' daily share-buyback limits for three months from November 24 and intensify monitoring of illegal short selling.

China's Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges will lower minimum margin requirements for stock purchases made with borrowed funds to 80% from 100% from November 30.

Chipmakers remain under pressure as investors reassess AI spending

SK Hynix fell 3.7%, Samsung Electronics lost 4.48% and LG Innotek slid 4.5%. In Taiwan, Largan Precision declined 3.3%, while Foxconn rose 0.6% and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. was little changed.

Chinese technology shares were mostly lower. Naura Technology plunged 8.9%, while Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. fell 2.5%, Cambricon Technologies lost 2.1% and Foxconn Industrial Internet declined 1.8%.

Tencent dropped 2.79%, Alibaba fell 4.02% and Meituan lost 4.14%; NetEase rose 2.79% and Goertek gained 1.57%.

"What could restore investors' confidence in the AI trade? In the past five years, mostly it was a positive catalyst from outside the chip industry. No superhero is needed. This time the biggest overhang is the Fed overtightening, so the rescue might have to come from the same source," said Anna Wu, investment strategist and founder at Floodline Research.

Meanwhile, treasury futures fell as demand for havens eased, while brent crude slipped as robust exports offset Middle East supply risks.

Wall Street futures jump after major indexes enter correction territory
